reordered reconnections, and concurrent reconnections from multiple client IPs.

## Design Links

- https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/SeqAnchor+SSE+design+doc
  - https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1s3SeqAnchor/proto-dumps

## Implementation Notes

- Protocol: add header X-Seq-Token on initial handshake; server will include 'anchor' SSE events with type=anchor and payload: {seq, boundary_type, boundary_id, checksum}.
  - Chunk envelope: each data chunk will be JSONL with fields: seq, offset, payload, checksum; payload may include function_call frames encoded separately and tagged with boundary_id.
  - Retention: keep last N anchors and associated chunks per stream; default retention window is 30s or 1MB. Configurable per-customer on Dedicated plans.
  - Resume logic: on reconnect with X-Seq-Resume, server validates seq and serves minimal replay window; if seq expired, fallback to full stream restart and emit 'resume_lost' event.
  - Idempotency for tool-calls: server assigns call-dedup-id for each function invocation; replays will not re-execute calls if dedup-id already seen—call status persisted to short-lived call cache with TTL aligned to retention window.
  - Compatibility shim: if client lacks resume headers, server emits a 'compat-v1' framing header and anchors will be no-op markers so older clients can ignore but preserve stream integrity.
  - Observability: emit telemetry events for resume_attempt, resume_success, resume_expired, anchor_emitted with stream_id and token; add dashboard panel in Console runtime-1.24.
  - API changes: SDKs (JS/Python/Go) will get helper util to persist resume token and transparently attempt resume; default enabled for hosted API, opt-out via client config.

(surface)
- Minimal calls: PrefetchManifest.upload(manifest), Handshake.status(session_token) and Cancel(prefetch_id). Rationale: small surface to maintain language SDK simplicity and reduce integration cost.
- SDKs expose local cache hooks: onManifestAccepted(metadata), onPrefetchProgress(percent), onFallback(reason).

Streaming interplay and structured output
- Manifest-driven prefetch allows server to start incremental partial outputs earlier (e.g., emit an initial structured header saying which tools are ready and which are degraded).
- Structured tool-calling frames include an optional prefetch.confirmation block that client SDK can use to render optimistic UI.

Telemetry and signals
- New metrics: prefetch.accept_rate, prefetch_hit_rate (per manifest entry), prefetch_latency_ms, prefetch_waste_tokens.
- Instrumentation: add prefetch.* tags to tracing spans and integrate with Console dashboards and Optimize recommendations.

Security and privacy
- Manifests may include private resource hints. Treat manifests as user data subject to retention/policy. Provide per-manifest privacy_tier: public|sensitive|restricted. Use KMS tagging for restricted prefetch jobs.

SDK ergonomics notes
- Lightweight: keep binary size small for mobile by providing manifest helpers as optional module.
- Backward compatible: manifest calls are optional; server falls back to default routing when absent.
- Offline-first: SDK should cache last manifest and attempt opportunistic prefetch when device is charging/wi-fi. Provide TTLs to prevent stale prefetches.

Operational concerns and rollout
- Canary feature flags per-customer to gate prefetch routing and billing. Initial limited rollout to 5 pilot customers.
- Billing: optional discounted prefetch token bucket (customer-paid) vs on-demand prefetch paid from normal usage. Need billing experiment.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- How to best express unknown/conditional flows (e.g., tool called only if search yield > 0)? Consider boolean predicates vs lightweight branching hints.
- Should prefetch be charged immediately or only when consumed? Need finance input (JIRA:PRIC-432).
- Tool init cost vs model warm: prioritize warm path ordering—policy decision.

Hi Ari —

Thanks again for joining the call today. Attached is a concise package with the recommended inference slate, basic benchmarks we ran against your sample prompt set, and a prompt pack you can use to validate outputs during the pilot (see attachments and Drive link below).

High-level recommended shortlist (for your evaluation sprint):

1) Redwood-Opt-13B (high-quality, moderate cost)
   - Strength: best blind-qa and instruction-following on your sample prompts (lowest error on extraction tasks).
   - Observed median p95 latency (128-token reply): ~98 ms on a shared 80GB GPU instance.
   - Unit cost: ~$0.80 per 1k output tokens (hosted); predictable in Dedicated.

2) Mistral-7B-Inst (quantized, cost-balanced)
   - Strength: strong quality for conversational flows, excellent throughput for short responses.
   - Observed median p95 latency (128-token reply): ~62 ms quantized on Ampere X; ~0.32 USD per 1k output tokens.
   - Good candidate for early pilot to reduce spend.

3) Redwood-Edge-3B (compact, latency/cost optimized)
   - Strength: lowest cost and fastest tail latency for short completions; acceptable for templated responses and reranking.
   - Observed median p95 latency (64-token reply): ~28 ms; ~0.08 USD per 1k output tokens.

Rationale notes:
- We prioritized models that cover the three operational tradeoffs you flagged on the call: (1) quality for extraction/QA, (2) cost per active user at scale, and (3) tail-latency for interactive workflows.
- The recommended path is: run parallel 2-week evals of Redwood-Opt-13B and Mistral-7B on your top 150 prompt variants, measure quality delta on your labeled set, and then gate the pilot on the crossover point where quality lift justifies cost.",

Connector: gmail

: recommended inference slate, benchmarks & next steps

Hi Ari —

Thanks again for joining the call today. Attached is a concise package with the recommended inference slate, basic benchmarks we ran against your sample prompt set, and a prompt pack you can use to validate outputs during the pilot (see attachments and Drive link below).

High-level recommended shortlist (for your evaluation sprint):

1) Redwood-Opt-13B (high-quality, moderate cost)
   - Strength: best blind-qa and instruction-following on your sample prompts (lowest error on extraction tasks).
   - Observed median p95 latency (128-token reply): ~98 ms on a shared 80GB GPU instance.
   - Unit cost: ~$0.80 per 1k output tokens (hosted); predictable in Dedicated.

2) Mistral-7B-Inst (quantized, cost-balanced)
   - Strength: strong quality for conversational flows, excellent throughput for short responses.
   - Observed median p95 latency (128-token reply): ~62 ms quantized on Ampere X; ~0.32 USD per 1k output tokens.
   - Good candidate for early pilot to reduce spend.

3) Redwood-Edge-3B (compact, latency/cost optimized)
   - Strength: lowest cost and fastest tail latency for short completions; acceptable for templated responses and reranking.
   - Observed median p95 latency (64-token reply): ~28 ms; ~0.08 USD per 1k output tokens.

Rationale notes:
- We prioritized models that cover the three operational tradeoffs you flagged on the call: (1) quality for extraction/QA, (2) cost per active user at scale, and (3) tail-latency for interactive workflows.
- The recommended path is: run parallel 2-week evals of Redwood-Opt-13B and Mistral-7B on your top 150 prompt variants, measure quality delta on your labeled set, and then gate the pilot on the crossover point where quality lift justifies cost.

ez: KMS integration is critical. Do you support customer-managed keys?
[04:01] Maya Chen: Yes, we support customer-managed keys for Private and Dedicated. For Hosted, we have a bring-your-own-key flow that integrates with major KMS providers — we'll include the docs.

--- Cost / latency tradeoffs and quantization ---
[04:15] Priya Nair: Cost is a big factor. If we choose a 32k model, token costs go up and GPU footprint too. How aggressive are your quantization recommendations?
[04:24] Jordan Patel: We have quantization profiles and will recommend per-model settings. For many production workloads, 4-bit quantized weights on certain kernels provide 2-3x cost reductions with limited quality loss, but some multilingual or instruction-following checkpoints regress. We always suggest a short eval to compare quality vs cost. Also automatic prefix/KV caching can cut token usage significantly for repeated contexts.
[04:50] Ethan Ruiz: What about throughput guarantees? If we go Dedicated, do we get predictable p99 latency?
[04:56] Jordan Patel: Yes — Dedicated comes with SLA-backed throughput and configurable autoscaling. You can define latency SLOs and fallback policies to cheaper model variants if the primary is overloaded.

--- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private decision factors ---
[05:15] Lina Ortega: From a product lens, we want fast experiments and then a stable production path. Hosted is fastest to test, Dedicated is predictable, Private is for strict compliance. Anything else to consider?

  - Cons: longer lead time to provision reserved GPUs, needs autoscaling policy tuning, some dev work to integrate tracing and rollout hooks.
  - When to pick: if the customer wants a predictable unit cost and an SLA they can rely on for demo and go-live.

3) Private (VPC / on-prem)
  - Pros: customer controls networking, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs under their tenancy, can meet strict compliance needs.
  - Cons: longest setup time, cross-team coordination, potential hardware procurement or network peering work, ops responsibilities shift to customer or SEP (professional services).

Workload fingerprinting (how we decide at run time):
- Step 1: Instrument initial hosted run with telemetry collection (token counts, seq length distribution, cold vs warm cache ratio, tail latencies per model).
- Step 2: After 7–10 days, compute the workload fingerprint (median seq length, top-5 prompt shapes, KV cache hit rate).
- Step 3: Use fingerprint to simulate Dedicated sizing (GPU type, batch size, expected throughput) and estimate per-token cost difference.
- Decision: if predicted dedicated cost <20% above hosted and latency improvement >35% at 95th, recommend Dedicated trial.

Latency/Cost estimation (ballpark for planning):
- Hosted: expected median latency 80–160ms (short prompts), 95th ~280–400ms depending on region; per-token cost baseline = $X* (customer billing TBD).
- Dedicated (A100-equivalent pool): median latency 30–90ms, 95th < 200ms under correct batching; per-token cost may drop 15–40% vs hosted at sufficient commit.
- Private: latency similar to Dedicated when colocated; incremental dev/ops costs significant.

Executive summary (2 lines): Redwood supports hosted, dedicated, and private modes. 2) Legal/technical controls for EU->US transfers:
- DPA Annex (SCCs equivalent): included as draft (see dpa_annex_draft_for_aurelia.pdf).
- Encryption: TLS1.2+ (recommended TLS1.3) in transit; AES-256-GCM at rest.

[03:50] Samir Patel: A couple of themes from the runs — first, more prescriptive runbooks per team; second, canaries need stricter gating thresholds; third, a small cross-functional pact to avoid emergency ad-hoc routing changes during high traffic windows.

[04:24] Elena Park: Also, on the org level, I don't want us shipping less. I want safer shipping. That means better automation and clearer boundaries: who approves what, and what rollbacks look like.

[05:02] Audience question (unlabeled): Is there a plan to change the on-call rotation length? The last on-call week felt rough.

[05:15] Diego Rivera: We're shortening the heavy-duty on-call block from 7 to 5 days for platform engineers and adding a secondary pager for database/net bursts; also adding an incident responder shadow for new hires. We want to reduce cognitive load.

[06:02] Maya Chen: On rollouts, proposing we add a gray release step for heavy models — a slow traffic ramp with explicit KV warming stage. It costs a bit but reduces rollback frequency.

[06:37] Aaron Kim: Cost note — a gray release and KV warmers will incur additional infra spend. We modeled the Q2 delta and it's about a mid single digit percent increase if we do this for all heavyweight deploys. But the reduction in urgent incident hours looks worth it.

[07:12] Ruth Gomez: From People perspective, we also need to balance time off for on-call. Hiring pipeline timing is important — we have offers out and need to close quickly to reduce on-call pressure.

[07:45] Elena Park: Quick hiring update — we're accelerating for critical infra roles but pausing new IC headcount elsewhere. This is tactical for the quarter; we want to ensure coverage where the SLO delta matters most.

emits structured audit events for console and runbooks.
- Add shadowing toggles for parallel probing of candidate variants without impacting live split.
- Provide an auto-rollback policy with hysteresis and graduated backoff to avoid flapping.
- Expose diagnostic endpoints and Grafana panels for per-step metrics and rationale.

Design highlights and novel ideas:
- "Safepoints": explicit named checkpoints in a rollout where non-reversible expansion requires additional approval or stronger signals. Safepoints can be configured as time-based or metric-based.
- "Horizon decay": a configurable attenuation function that slows traffic growth if variance in key metrics increases; helps prevent step overshoot for bursty workloads.
- Quality-aware splits: traffic weights can be dynamically rebalanced by integrating a lightweight quality signal (e.g., rerank drift or semantic similarity) for A/B tests.
- Shadow probes: sampled requests are mirrored to candidate variants with separate budget accounting; failures in the shadow path do not affect the live split but surface in the supervisor's risk score.

Acceptance criteria:
1) POST /rollouts accepts new spec and validates schema, including safepoints and attenuation curve.
2) Supervisor advances steps automatically when configured SLOs are met for a configurable consecutive window, and pauses when the guardrail is violated.
3) Automatic rollback triggers when sustained regression (configurable window) exceeds threshold; rollback includes a cooldown to prevent immediate reattempt.
4) Shadowing mode can be enabled per-route and produced mirrored telemetry tracked independently.
5) E2E integration tests added that simulate latency spikes, error bursts, and quality regressions and assert supervisor behavior.
6) Grafana dashboard with per-step metrics and an "explain" view (why step advanced/paused/rolled back).",

Guardchain template (ordered, automated-first):
1) Pre-flight (pre-deploy, checklist): unit tests, load profile simulation, synthetic traffic sanity run, feature flag gating.
2) Canary 0 (internal smoke): 0.1% internal traffic, auto-check: request success rate >= 99.9%, p95 latency < baseline+40ms, cost per token within +15%. Human: steward eyeballs logs.
3) Canary 1 (narrow external slice): 1% external slice, automated telemetry: response-quality metric (rerank CTR proxy / safety score) stable within corridor, automated anomaly detection (change point) negative. Human: product signoff if anomalies flagged.
4) Progression gates (automated): progressive exposure triggers only after sliding-window stability for 24h and no critical alerts for 1h.
5) Broader exposure (10–25%): automated A/B statistical checks for primary metric, guardchain enforces pause on drift > threshold or increased false positive rate.
6) Full activation + post-mortem schedule: final signoff and 72h observation plan.

Telemetry & signal design (examples):
- Performance: p50/p95/p99 latency, request success rate, queue/backpressure metrics, GPU utilization, batch sizes.
- Cost/capacity: tokens-in, tokens-out, cost per 1k tokens, unexpected synchronous falls back to CPU.
- Quality proxies: rerank CTR, downstream click-through, prompt-completion similarity to baseline (embedding distance), safety classifier score distributions.
- Slice-level deltas: compute per-slice deltas for above metrics (region, device, org size).
- Signal windows: sliding windows: 5m, 1h, 24h for different gates.",

## Acceptance Criteria

- Sampler can select probes across three strata with per-cohort configurable rates and expose sampling metrics to tracing.
  - Composite score computed in real-time and stored per-request with an explanatory breakdown (semantic, token-accuracy, latency penalty) for debugging.
  - Policy engine supports three remediation actions: throttle, divert-to-fallback, pause-and-escalate; each action must be auditable and reversible.
  - Automated tests and chaos tests demonstrate rollback only occurs after two independent metric family failures within sliding window and not for single noisy drops.
  - Console view shows last 100 probe results, probe coverage heatmap, and allows SRE/PM to tune weights and thresholds for specific cohorts.

## Technical Design

- Probe ingestion: lightweight agent in serving path annotates requests when sampled; heavy-weight probes run in parallel worker pool to avoid blocking main request path.
  - Score computation: streaming aggregation using existing metrics pipeline (Kafka -> Flink -> scoring service) with per-customer state kept in Redis for short-window hysteresis checks.
  - Policy engine: extension of rollout-conductor that accepts composite-scores and issues actions via existing route-control APIs; actions recorded to audit log and event bus.
  - Privacy: customer probes that may include PII are redacted at ingestion and evaluated in private-only mode for Private deployments; sampling rates default to 0 for sensitive customers until explicitly enabled.
  - Backfills: ability to run historical probe replays against a model snapshot for offline validation and to populate baseline distributions used by the gating logic.

emits structured audit events for console and runbooks.
- Add shadowing toggles for parallel probing of candidate variants without impacting live split.
- Provide an auto-rollback policy with hysteresis and graduated backoff to avoid flapping.
- Expose diagnostic endpoints and Grafana panels for per-step metrics and rationale.

Design highlights and novel ideas:
- "Safepoints": explicit named checkpoints in a rollout where non-reversible expansion requires additional approval or stronger signals. Safepoints can be configured as time-based or metric-based.
- "Horizon decay": a configurable attenuation function that slows traffic growth if variance in key metrics increases; helps prevent step overshoot for bursty workloads.
- Quality-aware splits: traffic weights can be dynamically rebalanced by integrating a lightweight quality signal (e.g., rerank drift or semantic similarity) for A/B tests.
- Shadow probes: sampled requests are mirrored to candidate variants with separate budget accounting; failures in the shadow path do not affect the live split but surface in the supervisor's risk score.

Acceptance criteria:
1) POST /rollouts accepts new spec and validates schema, including safepoints and attenuation curve.
2) Supervisor advances steps automatically when configured SLOs are met for a configurable consecutive window, and pauses when the guardrail is violated.
3) Automatic rollback triggers when sustained regression (configurable window) exceeds threshold; rollback includes a cooldown to prevent immediate reattempt.
4) Shadowing mode can be enabled per-route and produced mirrored telemetry tracked independently.
5) E2E integration tests added that simulate latency spikes, error bursts, and quality regressions and assert supervisor behavior.
6) Grafana dashboard with per-step metrics and an "explain" view (why step advanced/paused/rolled back).

- Data/Analytics: provides baseline metric instrumentation and quick-turn queries for emergent slices.
- Trust & Safety / Legal: auto-invoked for high-sensitivity slices or new tool-calling features.

Guardchain template (ordered, automated-first):
1) Pre-flight (pre-deploy, checklist): unit tests, load profile simulation, synthetic traffic sanity run, feature flag gating.
2) Canary 0 (internal smoke): 0.1% internal traffic, auto-check: request success rate >= 99.9%, p95 latency < baseline+40ms, cost per token within +15%. Human: steward eyeballs logs.
3) Canary 1 (narrow external slice): 1% external slice, automated telemetry: response-quality metric (rerank CTR proxy / safety score) stable within corridor, automated anomaly detection (change point) negative. Human: product signoff if anomalies flagged.
4) Progression gates (automated): progressive exposure triggers only after sliding-window stability for 24h and no critical alerts for 1h.
5) Broader exposure (10–25%): automated A/B statistical checks for primary metric, guardchain enforces pause on drift > threshold or increased false positive rate.
6) Full activation + post-mortem schedule: final signoff and 72h observation plan.

Telemetry & signal design (examples):
- Performance: p50/p95/p99 latency, request success rate, queue/backpressure metrics, GPU utilization, batch sizes.
- Cost/capacity: tokens-in, tokens-out, cost per 1k tokens, unexpected synchronous falls back to CPU.
- Quality proxies: rerank CTR, downstream click-through, prompt-completion similarity to baseline (embedding distance), safety classifier score distributions.
- Slice-level deltas: compute per-slice deltas for above metrics (region, device, org size).
- Signal windows: sliding windows: 5m, 1h, 24h for different gates.

Quick triage notes for the A vs B variant comparison run (eval-run-2026-04-01-variantB-vs-A). This doc focuses on the emergent instruction-drift signal we observed during the onboarding evals and a compact win/loss breakdown across prompt families. Goal: decide whether to proceed with a small canary, add targeted mitigations, or hold rollout.

Top-line numbers (aggregate):
- Overall pairwise win-rate (respecting majority human preference): Variant B wins 61%, Variant A wins 39% (n=5,200 pairwise judgments across prompt panels).
- Instruction-drift index (IDI): +4.2 pts for Variant B vs A (higher = more deviation from explicit instructions on constrained tasks).

Evaluation protocol recap:
- Prompt families: code-completion (long), interactive-chat, factual-QA (finance+health subsets), multi-step reasoning, summarization (long doc), instruction-follow (constrained/vs open).
- Sampling: stratified by family; human pairwise judgments for a 5k sample set (balanced across families).
- Automatic metrics: BLEU/ROUGE where applicable, Toxicity (Perspective API proxy), Self-consistency consistency score, hallucination detector (heuristic+model).
- Safety panel: a 1k subset manually reviewed by safety team.

Compact win/loss table (human pref pairwise) — top families:
- Instruction-follow (constrained): A wins 72 / B wins 28 (A stronger at obeying exact step limits).
- Multi-step reasoning: B wins 68 / A wins 32 (B better at chaining reasoning but more stray assumptions).
- Factual QA (finance subset): B wins 55 / A wins 45

mina: sample sizes: long-answer ~480 reqs per 30m. using bootstrap CI we see lower bound ~-3.4% so non-trivial. proposing these rules:

- canary windows: 20m

## Acceptance Criteria

- Sampler can select probes across three strata with per-cohort configurable rates and expose sampling metrics to tracing.
  - Composite score computed in real-time and stored per-request with an explanatory breakdown (semantic, token-accuracy, latency penalty) for debugging.
  - Policy engine supports three remediation actions: throttle, divert-to-fallback, pause-and-escalate; each action must be auditable and reversible.
  - Automated tests and chaos tests demonstrate rollback only occurs after two independent metric family failures within sliding window and not for single noisy drops.
  - Console view shows last 100 probe results, probe coverage heatmap, and allows SRE/PM to tune weights and thresholds for specific cohorts.

## Technical Design

- Probe ingestion: lightweight agent in serving path annotates requests when sampled; heavy-weight probes run in parallel worker pool to avoid blocking main request path.
  - Score computation: streaming aggregation using existing metrics pipeline (Kafka -> Flink -> scoring service) with per-customer state kept in Redis for short-window hysteresis checks.
  - Policy engine: extension of rollout-conductor that accepts composite-scores and issues actions via existing route-control APIs; actions recorded to audit log and event bus.
  - Privacy: customer probes that may include PII are redacted at ingestion and evaluated in private-only mode for Private deployments; sampling rates default to 0 for sensitive customers until explicitly enabled.
  - Backfills: ability to run historical probe replays against a model snapshot for offline validation and to populate baseline distributions used by the gating logic.

- Unit tests: normalization math, edge cases (zero vectors), deterministic paths for CPU/GPU.

  - Canary experiments: measure MRR and NDCG on internal reranking eval set and compare to baseline. Auto-fail deployment if quality drops >1% or latency p95 increases >20%.
  - Compatibility tests: stored-embedding lookup tests where stored vectors were produced by older server versions.

x speedup for weight-load bound kernels on GPU with INT8 weights + FP16 activations
  - Latency p95 change: <= +5ms relative to current FP16 baseline (hard guard)
  - Model size reduction: weight memory savings ~2x compared to FP16 baseline

## Benchmarks And Results

- Initial microbenchmarks (internal, 2026-03-10) on text-embed-4-small: mean_cosine = 0.9961, median_drop = 0.28%, recall@10 drop = 0.6%
  - KV cache sanity: no observed corruption when activations run in FP16 and weights are INT8 in synthetic trace test
  - Throughput test on A100-80GB: 1.9x token/sec improvement for embedding forward pass when using INT8 weights
  - Edge case: outlier-heavy biology dataset showed mean cosine 0.992 -> added 99.99th percentile calibration option

## Risks And Mitigations

- Risk: calibration corpus not representative —> Mitigation: include automated sampling from production (anonymized) and maintain per-customer test slices
  - Risk: rare precision regressions for certain queries —> Mitigation: implement per-request fallback to FP16/FP32 if validation probe sample falls below threshold
  - Risk: quantized artifacts incompatible with older runtime kernels —> Mitigation: add artifact manifest with runtime-min-version and compatibility checks in deploy pipeline
  - Risk: evaluation benchmark doesn't reflect real retrieval downstream —> Mitigation: run AB tests on 1% traffic with canary and monitor downstream KPIs

## Rollout Plan

Sensitivity: hallucination-sensitive (needs external facts/IDs), safety-sensitive (toxicity risk), low-risk
- Context length bucket: short (<64 tokens), mid (64–512), long (>512)
This yields interpretable slices like: "short-answer-hallucination-sensitive", "long-form-low-risk", "multi-turn-chat-mid-length".

Metrics (definitions used here):
- Semantic Perturbation Score (SPS): 0–100 scale derived from entailment + embedding similarity + normalized token overlap; lower is worse. We report delta = quantized minus fp16.
- Prompt Robustness Index (PRI): percentage of runs where the top-3 completions overlap by >=0.7 cosine and operator acceptability; captures stability to sampling and numeric instability.
- Hallucination Drift Rate (HDR): fraction of responses with unsupported factual claims relative to a small knowledge oracle (wiki-snapshot) — flagged by our internal hallucination detector.
- Latency and token-cost deltas included but considered secondary for this doc.

Methodology (concise):
- Prompt set: 1,200 prompts selected from onboarding pool (balanced by product route and historical failure log).
- Runs: 5 seeds per prompt with sampling settings matching production (temperature 0.2–0.7 depending on route), deterministic evaluation for QA slices where applicable.
- Post-process: automatic metrics + 300 human spot checks (stratified across slices).
- Hardware: A100 fp16 baseline; quantized models executed on testbench nodes with kernels closest to production environment.

Detailed per-slice notes (selected slices with notable deltas):
1) short-answer-hallucination-sensitive
   - SPS delta: AWQ-8 -2.1, GPTQ-8 -3.0, int8 -4.5, int4 -12.8
   - PRI delta: AWQ -3%, GPTQ -6%, int8 -8%, int4 -28%
   - HDR: AWQ +1.8ppt, GPTQ +3

result.title: Synthetic schedule and evidence playbook for SLO drift
result.text:
[Document context]
Title: Synthetic schedule and evidence playbook for SLO drift
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/synthetic-schedule-and-evidence-playbook-for-slo-drift-2026.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: oncall-and-incident-response

CS) + Incident Owner.

Definitions & thresholds:
- SLO drift alert: 15m p95 latency > target * 1.25 OR token error-rate increase > +0.5 percentage points vs baseline.
- Baseline: rolling 7d median of the metric at the same hour-of-day.

Detection & synthetic schedule (recommended):
Run synthetic probes targeted at representative routes and model sizes. Schedule below is minimum — increase cadence for high-risk releases.

| Probe | Target | Frequency | Owner | Success criteria |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Quick-chat (short inputs) | chat-route-prod | 1m | Synthetics team | p95 < 200ms + no partial-token errors |
| Long-context generation (2k tokens) | gen-long-prod | 5m | Synthetics team | median < 800ms + token-error-rate < 0.5% |
| Embedding consistency | embed-prod | 15m | Synthetics team | vector-norm deviation < 0.01 vs baseline |

Evidence collection checklist (first 30 minutes):
1) Mark alert and assign incident owner.
2) Snapshot: capture 15m and 1h windows for affected metrics (p50/p95 latency, error-rate, queue-length).
3) Pull traces for 95th percentile requests and representative successful/failed traces.
4) Collect synthetic probe results and full payloads for last 2h.
5) Record rollout metadata: model version(s), routing policy, recent canaries, autoscaling events, new infra patches.
6) Note correlated signals: infra CPU/GPU utilization, network egress errors, backing-store latencies (KV, DB), throttling events.

delta for 768-dim vectors (within tolerance).
  - 2026-03-14: Began canary rollout on eu-west-1 with normalize=false default and normalize opt-in enabled via feature flag. Observing baseline latency impact of ~7% on sample traffic.

## Risks And Mitigation

- Risk: Customers will unknowingly mix normalized and unnormalized embeddings leading to low-quality reranking. Mitigation: add strict cache headers, telemetry alerts for mixed-reads, and an 'incompatibility' warning in the console when queries mix metrics.
  - Risk: Normalization kernel increases p99 latency under heavy batching. Mitigation: implement adaptive path that skips per-request normalization for large batches and instead runs an async normalization job when possible; provide autoscale knobs.
  - Risk: Quantization amplifies numeric drift. Mitigation: tighten acceptance tests for quantized modes and document expected deltas. Offer a 'force-recompute' migration utility for high-precision customers.
  - Risk: Backwards compatibility regressions. Mitigation: nightly matrix includes legacy client tests and we keep default behavior unchanged unless 'normalize=true' is passed.

## Testing Plan

- Unit tests: normalization math, edge cases (zero vectors), deterministic paths for CPU/GPU.
  - Integration tests: embeddings->rerank flow with both normalize=true and normalize=false across quantized/unquantized models.
  - Performance tests: microbenchmarks for kernel on representative instance types (p3, p4, infer-rt specialized HW), end-to-end load tests for common batch sizes.
  - Canary experiments: measure MRR and NDCG on internal reranking eval set and compare to baseline. Auto-fail deployment if quality drops >1% or latency p95 increases >20%.
  - Compatibility tests: stored-embedding lookup tests where stored vectors were produced by older server versions.

## Docs And Rollout Tasks

Content: Purpose:
Sketch for a lightweight, cross-functional canary matrix we can run for LLM features that balances cost/latency safety and behavioral quality. This is intentionally compact — a fieldable checklist + signal mapping that multiple teams (product, SRE, research, solutions) can rally around without heavy ceremony.

High-level idea (one-liner):
Create an "activation mosaic": a small set of orthogonal exposure slices (latency-sensitive, cost-bound, quality-sensitive, geographic/regulatory) and a signal-to-action matrix that maps measured telemetry to deterministic human+automated responses.

Why this instead of a single canary flow?
- LLM features have heterogeneous failure modes: latency spikes, token-cost escalations, semantic drift/hallucinations, content-safety regressions. One axis of traffic doesn't capture multi-dimensional risk.
- Cross-team clarity: each slice owns a primary signal and an escalation path so SRE, product, and ML know what to act on.

Canvas (core components):
- Slices (examples):
  - Slice A: Latency-sensitive (mobile users, short prompts)
  - Slice B: Cost-bound (large-batch embeddings or background inference)
  - Slice C: Quality-watch (prompt templates tied to user-facing responses)
  - Slice D: Safety/Regulatory (EU region, PII-sensitive endpoints)
  - Slice E: Synthetic stress (synthetic traffic for worst-case sequences)

- Primary signals per slice (what we watch first):
  - Latency-sensitive: p95 latency, tail qps per model-worker, CPU/GPU queue depth
  - Cost-bound: per-token cost rate, inference VM utilization per project, sudden increase in avg tokens per request
  - Quality-watch: hallucination rate (eval set comparisons), user feedback rate (thumbs down), rerank degradation
  - Safety/Regulatory: content filter hit-rate, KMS errors, audit-log gaps
  - Synthetic stress: error-rate under synthetic tokens, KV cache eviction rate, memory OOMs

_NVTX=1; ./bin/serve --config cfg.json & sleep 5; ./tools/nvprof_collect.sh pid
- quick microbench: python tools/kernel_probe.py --model llama13b --kernel fused-coalesce-aggressive --seq 512 --batch 1 --reps 1000

Preliminary results (summary)
- Baseline (flash-v1, no-slicing, conservative-fuse): p95 token latency ~ 48ms, p99 ~ 82ms on A10g, median ~ 18ms. GPU util ~72%.
- Slicing=4 + conservative-fuse: p95 down to 36ms, p99 down to 63ms, median increases slightly to 20ms; tokens/sec -3%. Observed fewer large queuing spikes in host-side queue depth plots.
- Slicing=4 + aggressive-fuse: p95 30ms, p99 55ms, median 22ms; tokens/sec -6% (some throughput loss). GPU registers and shared memory utilization higher by ~12% in Nsight snapshots.
- Paged-attn (page=64) without rebase buffer + slicing: flash-v2 kernels show 10–18% slower per-kernel times relative to contiguous case; p99 regresses by ~15ms.
- Paged-attn + small defrag rebase (copy into contiguous staging buffer for slice): overhead ~2–4ms per token but restores kernel throughput; net p99 wins when slice size > 3 pages.

Notable traces and artifacts
- NVTX trace: nvtx-run-2025-08-20-2.json — shows host-queue spikes at t=120s correlating with p99 spikes.
- Nsight capture: nsight-burst-aug21 captures register-pressure during fused-aggressive kernels where kernel runtime has variable stalls.
- Kernel-probe outputs: kernel-probe-512x1-fused-aggr.csv — shows tail latency of matmul-softmax fusion rising when free blocks < threshold.

benchmark (bench/embeds/pipeline) shows <=5% token cost increase or improved cost per embedding

## Steps

- 1) Reproduce p99 in controlled environment using continuous-replay of production request traces (w/ secrets scrubbed)
  - 2) Baseline: capture current micro-batch coalescing latencies, kernel startup times, and GPU occupancy profiles (perfetto + nsys)
  - 3) Implement adaptive coalescing: dynamic window that shortens on high concurrency and lengthens on low RPS (feature branch)
  - 4) Kernel tuning: switch hot paths to optimized fused-kernels for common model shapes, adjust launch parameters for sm_80+ GPUs, compare quantized vs fp16 kernels
  - 5) Add warm-up shim for first requests to mitigate cold-kernel overhead on newly spun workers
  - 6) Run end-to-end benchmarks (p50/p95/p99) and embedding-quality regression tests
  - 7) Canary rollout (10% traffic) with tight alerting: p99 increase > 10% triggers automated rollback
  - 8) Full rollout with staged ramp and post-rollout review

Smoke test prompts (short list — run 3x each):
- Summarize: "Summarize the following paragraph in 20 words or less:" (checks truncation)

- Safety: content moderation quick checks (should be allowed neutral content)

Night-shift heuristics / notes to conductor (informal):
- Be conservative in first 45 minutes; transient noise common when caches refill.
- If multiple small signals appear (latency + small error bump + memory drift) treat as composite -> pause ramp.
- Keep direct comm lines open; escalate early. Better to pause than to roll forward blind.
- Use the pinned slack thread for every decision (time-stamped).

Open questions / TODOs (sticking points to resolve pre-latch):
- Who is owner for content-quality gating automation? (Samira suggested a lightweight scripts run; needs signoff.)

- Add small synthetic that triggers known edge-case in parser v1.9 (we have a mocked sample, need to add to smoke set).

Post-latch handoff (format for morning summary):
- Short header: Rollout start time, final traffic %, rollback? (Y/N)
- Key signals: P95 delta, error delta, notable infra events
- Forensics pointers: link to replay buffer + top 20 failed request ids
- Action items: triage owners + ETA

    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Streaming handshake, compact frames, and SDK resume - PRD (wip)\",\n  \"owner\": \"Priya Patel\",\n  \"drive_area\": \"shared_drives\",\n  \"path\": \"shared_drives/product/hosted-api/streaming-handshake-compact-frames-and-sdk-resume-prd-wip.json\",\n  \"doc_type\": \"doc\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-11-03\",\n  \"last_modified\": \"2025-11-18\",\n  \"status\": \"draft\",\n  \"team\": \"product-hosted-api\",\n  \"collaborators\": [\n    \"Miguel Rivera\",\n    \"Ava Thompson\",\n    \"Jordan Lee\",\n    \"Eleanor Chen\"\n  ],\n  \"tags\": [\n    \"streaming\",\n    \"sdk\",\n    \"tool-calling\",\n    \"structured-output\",\n    \"resume\",\n    \"handshake\",\n    \"backpressure\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_artifacts\": [\n    \"https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/ENG-4821\",\n    \"https://github.com/redwood-inference/hosted-api/pull/818\",\n    \"confluence:/hosting/streaming-handshake-spec-v1\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"Summary:\\\\n\\\\nThis doc proposes a compact streaming handshake and frame format to support low-latency token streams, structured tool-calls, and resumable sessions at the SDK level. The goal is a minimal server-client protocol that: reduces per-frame overhead, allows safe partial validation of structured outputs on the client, supports durable resume/checkpoint semantics for flaky networks, and keeps SDK ergonomics simple for product engineers.\\\\n\\\\nWhy this exists (motivation):\\\\n- Customers are building interactive experiences where partial results can trigger UI updates or downstream tool calls as soon as possible.\\\\n- Current streaming options either send raw deltas (fast but untyped) or large JSON blobs (safe but high latency).\\\\n- SDK authors want a single high-level API that works across: simple text streaming, structured JSON outputs, and tool call handoffs, without forcing app teams to re-implement complex resume and validation logic.\\\\n\\\\nPrimary goals:\\\\n- Compact frame model with typed frames (open, chunk, tool-call, checkpoint, error, close).\\\\n- Handshake negotiation for capabilities (schema validation, resume tokens, chunk checksums).\\\\n- SDK surface that exposes: an async iterator for low-level streaming, plus a high-level callback/handler model for tool frames and validated objects.\\\\n- A resumable checkpoint protocol that is idempotent and minimizes re-computation for client apps.\\\\n- Clear security and privacy constraints for tool-calls and checkpoint persistence.\\\\n\\\\nNon-goals:\\\\n- Replacing full session storage / long-term logs (we aim for short-lived resume tokens, not permanent persistence).\\\\n- Complex on-server validation for every partial; server may annotate frames but client retains responsibility for final validation decisions.\\\\n\\\\nRequirements (must-have):\\\\n- Negotiated frames: server and client can advertise supported frame types and version (v1).\\\\n- Frames are small and parseable without full JSON parse for the common text streaming path.\\\\n- Tool-call frames must include a minimal typed descriptor so SDKs can either route to a tool handler or buffer until validated.\\\\n- Checkpoints (resume tokens) must be cryptographically-backed brief tokens (signed, expiry) to avoid server-side state explosion.\\\\n- Backpressure primitive: client can signal desired buffer size / max-inflight-chunks at handshake and dynamically via flow-control frames.\\\\n\\\\nNice-to-have (stretch):\\\\n- Optional delta-compression for chat context updates in high-throughput clients.\\\\n- Server-originated checkpoints for long-running sessions to allow cheaper resume on reconnect.\\\\n\\\\nProtocol proposal (high-level):\\\\n- Transport: HTTPS / HTTP2 streaming or WebSocket for interactive use cases. Servers must support both; clients choose based on environment.\\\\n- Negotiation: initial HTTP headers / WS message contain: protocol_version, supported_frame_types, resume_capability (true/false), max_chunk_bytes_hint.\\\\n- Frames: binary-ish but JSON-lite shapes encoded as UTF-8 lines (newline-delimited). Keep it human readable for debugging while smaller than full nested JSON.\\\\n\\\\nFrame types (v1):\\\\n1) OPEN_STREAM: {stream_id, features:[\\\\\\\"resume\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"schema_v1\\\\\\\"], schema_hash?} - server or client can send to start; server replies with OPEN_ACK.\\\\n2) TEXT_CHUNK: {seq, stream_id, bytes, final:bool} - raw token chunk (commonly used). Minimal header then raw bytes.\\\\n3) STRUCT_FRAME: {seq, stream_id, path, truncated:bool, checksum?} - for typed output fragments (path = JSON path being built). Allows incremental validation.\\\\n4) TOOL_CALL: {seq, stream_id, tool_id, params_ref, confidence, meta} - indicates a candidate tool invocation. SDK may accept or reject. params_ref can be a small blob or pointer to a subsequent DATA_BLOB.\\\\n5) DATA_BLOB: {id, format:json|binary, size, chunk_payload} - carries larger metadata or tool params when embedding directly.\\\\n6) CHECKPOINT: {stream_id, token, seq, signature, meta} - resume token emitted by server (or requested by client), short-lived.\\\\n7) FLOW_CONTROL: {stream_id, window_bytes} - client or server can adjust flow control.\\\\n8) ERROR_FRAME: {stream_id, seq, code, message} - terminal/non-terminal errors.\\\\n9) CLOSE_STREAM: {stream_id, reason} - end.\\\\n\\\\nNotes on STRUCT_FRAME and partial validation:\\\\n- The server can annotate which JSON path is completed in the current chunk so SDKs can run partial validators (e.g., \\\\\\\"title\\\\\\\" field done). We avoid sending large object parents until necessary.\\\\n- Clients should be able to subscribe to path-level events (SDK API will expose simple callbacks like onField(path, valuePart)).\\\\n\\\\nResume semantics and tokens:\\\\n- CHECKPOINT tokens are compact JWT-like strings signed by Redwood's streaming service with embedded: stream_id, last_seq, expiry, checksum of last N bytes.\\\\n- On reconnect, client re-OPENs with resume_token. Server verifies signature and if valid, emits a CHECKPOINT_REPLAY that includes omitted frames to catch-up or signals that replay not possible (then fallback to start-from-scratch).\\\\n- Tokens are short-lived (default 5 minutes) to avoid long-term state. Policy can be configurable per-customer.\\\\n\\\\nSDK ergonomics (JS/TS first-pass):\\\\n- Low-level: createStream(opts) returns AsyncIterable<Frame> and a controller with methods: send() (for client frames), requestResume(token), setWindow(bytes). This is for advanced use.\\\\n- High-level: StreamClient.open({schema, onText, onStruct, onTool, onCheckpoint, onError}) where handlers are simple sync/async functions. The SDK will manage checksums, resume attempts, and flow-control automatically.\\\\n- Tool registration: client.registerTool({id, handler: (params) => Promise<Result>, timeout}) - SDK routes TOOL_CALL frames to handlers. If no handler, SDK buffers until app decides.\\\\n- Validation mode: open|partial|strict. In partial mode, SDK emits onStruct events when enough path fragments arrive. In strict mode, SDK will attempt to reconstruct and run schema validation and emit error frames if mismatch.\\\\n\\\\nBackpressure and latency tradeoffs: \\\\n- Default client window 64KB. If app needs lower latency, pass max_window_bytes=8KB.\\\\n- SDK will apply jittered retries on resume to avoid thundering herd.\\\\n\\\\nSecurity & privacy considerations:\\\\n- Checkpoints should not include PII. If model output contains sensitive info, servers should redact before embedding into resume checksums.\\\\n- Tool-calls may include secrets in params; SDK must mark them ephemeral and not persist them in local storage unless explicitly requested by the app.\\\\n- Resume tokens must be signed and short-lived; no server-side sticky state required.\\\\n\\\\nTelemetry and observability (minimal):\\\\n- Events: stream.open, stream.resume_attempt, stream.resume_success, stream.resume_fail, tool.call, validation.failure, flow_control_change, stream.close.\\\\n- Recommended sample rates: resume events 100%, validation failures 100%, text_chunk histograms 1% by default.\\\\n\\\\nMigration and rollout plan:\\\\n- Phase 0 (internal): implement server v1 behind experiment flag + JS SDK prototype, test with 2 internal apps.\\\\n- Phase 1 (beta): opt-in customers, provide client library with feature flag header: X-RW-Stream-Pro: compact-v1.\\\\n- Phase 2 (GA): turn on for hosted-api streaming default for new models; provide backwards-compatible fallback that accepts plain newline-delimited text for older clients.\\\\n\\\\nOpen questions / TODOs:\\\\n- How large should CHECKPOINT's embedded checksum window be? (8KB vs 32KB?) - Eng to benchmark.\\\\n- Should DATA_BLOB be chunked separately (for large params) or force params_ref pattern to encourage pointer-based tool calls?\\\\n- UX for partial schema errors: should SDK automatically ask server for a re-generation or surface raw failure to the app?\\\\n- Interop with existing typed-tool-contracts (PRD cross-check needed).\\\\n\\\\nNext steps / action items:\\\\n- Miguel: prototype server framing layer and handshake negotiation (ENG-4821) - due 2025-12-08.\\\\n- Ava: JS SDK prototype (async iterator + high-level callback API) and sample app wiring for tool routing - due 2025-12-12.\\\\n- Priya (owner): Draft developer playbook + beta opt-in docs for Console and API docs, add telemetry events mapping - due 2025-12-18.\\\\n- Jordan: security review and resume token format design - due 2025-12-15.\\\\n\\\\nAppendix (sketch of handshake example):\\\\n1) Client -> POST /v1/streams (headers: X-RW-Stream-Pro: compact-v1, Accept: text/ndjson) body: OPEN_STREAM( {features:[\\\\\\\"resume\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"schema_v1\\\\\\\"], schema_hash:\\\\\\\"sha256:abc\\\\\\\"} )\\\\n2) Server -> OPEN_ACK {stream_id: \\\\\\\"s-123\\\\\\\", max_window: 65536}\\\\n3) Server -> TEXT_CHUNK(seq:1, bytes: \\\\\\\"Hello \\\\\\\")\\\\n4) Server -> STRUCT_FRAME(seq:2, path: \\\\\\\"user.name\\\\\\\", truncated:false, bytes:\\\\\\\"Ava\\\\\\\")\\\\n5) Server -> TOOL_CALL(seq:3, tool_id:\\\\\\\"search\\\\\\\", params_ref: \\\\\\\"b-42\\\\\\\")\\\\n6) Server -> DATA_BLOB(id:\\\\\\\"b-42\\\\\\\", format:json, chunk_payload:\\\\\\\"{\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"query\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"redwood streaming\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"}\\\\\\\")\\\\n7) Server -> CHECKPOINT(seq:3, token:\\\\\\\"eyJhbGciOi...\\\\\\\", signature: \\\\\\\"sig\\\\\\\")\\\\n\\\\nWe keep the doc intentionally compact rather than full PRD. This file is a synthesis of product + eng tradeoffs; aim is to surface a pragmatic path that reduces overhead for common text-first uses while enabling structured outputs and resume semantics without heavy server-side storage.\\\\n\\\\nNotes to self: add a quick compatibility table comparing this to existing typed-streaming proposals (follow up with doc cross-link).\\\\n\\\\n\",\n  \"__comment_placeholder\": \"Do not delete - keeps JSON friendly for downstream parsers\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_a36ff6948cce43c2b1bf1f5150d19996\"\n}",

    {
      "id": "dsid_a36ff6948cce43c2b1bf1f5150d19996:00001",

      "ordinal": 1,
      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Streaming handshake, compact frames, and SDK resume - PRD (wip)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/product/hosted-api/streaming-handshake-compact-frames-and-sdk-resume-prd-wip.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: product-hosted-api\n\nContent: Summary:\\n\\nThis doc proposes a compact streaming handshake and frame format to support low-latency token streams, structured tool-calls, and resumable sessions at the SDK level. The goal is a minimal server-client protocol that: reduces per-frame overhead, allows safe partial validation of structured outputs on the client, supports durable resume/checkpoint semantics for flaky networks, and keeps SDK ergonomics simple for product engineers.\\n\\nWhy this exists (motivation):\\n- Customers are building interactive experiences where partial results can trigger UI updates or downstream tool calls as soon as possible.\\n- Current streaming options either send raw deltas (fast but untyped) or large JSON blobs (safe but high latency).\\n- SDK authors want a single high-level API that works across: simple text streaming, structured JSON outputs, and tool call handoffs, without forcing app teams to re-implement complex resume and validation logic.\\n\\nPrimary goals:\\n- Compact frame model with typed frames (open, chunk, tool-call, checkpoint, error, close).\\n- Handshake negotiation for capabilities (schema validation, resume tokens, chunk checksums).\\n- SDK surface that exposes: an async iterator for low-level streaming, plus a high-level callback/handler model for tool frames and validated objects.\\n- A resumable checkpoint protocol that is idempotent and minimizes re-computation for client apps.\\n- Clear security and privacy constraints for tool-calls and checkpoint persistence.\\n\\nNon-goals:\\n- Replacing full session storage / long-term logs (we aim for short-lived resume tokens, not permanent persistence).\\n- Complex on-server validation for every partial; server may annotate frames but client retains responsibility for final validation decisions.\\n\\nRequirements (must-have):\\n- Negotiated frames: server and client can advertise supported frame types and version (v1).\\n- Frames are small and parseable without full JSON parse for the common text streaming path.\\n- Tool-call frames must include a minimal typed descriptor so SDKs can either route to a tool handler or buffer until validated.\\n- Checkpoints (resume tokens)",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Streaming handshake, compact frames, and SDK resume - PRD (wip)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/product/hosted-api/streaming-handshake-compact-frames-and-sdk-resume-prd-wip.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: product-hosted-api\n\ncan advertise supported frame types and version (v1).\\n- Frames are small and parseable without full JSON parse for the common text streaming path.\\n- Tool-call frames must include a minimal typed descriptor so SDKs can either route to a tool handler or buffer until validated.\\n- Checkpoints (resume tokens) must be cryptographically-backed brief tokens (signed, expiry) to avoid server-side state explosion.\\n- Backpressure primitive: client can signal desired buffer size / max-inflight-chunks at handshake and dynamically via flow-control frames.\\n\\nNice-to-have (stretch):\\n- Optional delta-compression for chat context updates in high-throughput clients.\\n- Server-originated checkpoints for long-running sessions to allow cheaper resume on reconnect.\\n\\nProtocol proposal (high-level):\\n- Transport: HTTPS / HTTP2 streaming or WebSocket for interactive use cases. Servers must support both; clients choose based on environment.\\n- Negotiation: initial HTTP headers / WS message contain: protocol_version, supported_frame_types, resume_capability (true/false), max_chunk_bytes_hint.\\n- Frames: binary-ish but JSON-lite shapes encoded as UTF-8 lines (newline-delimited). Keep it human readable for debugging while smaller than full nested JSON.\\n\\nFrame types (v1):\\n1) OPEN_STREAM: {stream_id, features:[\\\"resume\\\",\\\"schema_v1\\\"], schema_hash?} - server or client can send to start; server replies with OPEN_ACK.\\n2) TEXT_CHUNK: {seq, stream_id, bytes, final:bool} - raw token chunk (commonly used). Minimal header then raw bytes.\\n3) STRUCT_FRAME: {seq, stream_id, path, truncated:bool, checksum?} - for typed output fragments (path = JSON path being built). Allows incremental validation.\\n4) TOOL_CALL: {seq, stream_id, tool_id, params_ref, confidence, meta} - indicates a candidate tool invocation. SDK may accept or reject. params_ref can be a small blob or pointer to a subsequent DATA_BLOB.\\n5) DATA_BLOB: {id, format:",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Streaming handshake, compact frames, and SDK resume - PRD (wip)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/product/hosted-api/streaming-handshake-compact-frames-and-sdk-resume-prd-wip.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: product-hosted-api\n\n.\\n4) TOOL_CALL: {seq, stream_id, tool_id, params_ref, confidence, meta} - indicates a candidate tool invocation. SDK may accept or reject. params_ref can be a small blob or pointer to a subsequent DATA_BLOB.\\n5) DATA_BLOB: {id, format:json|binary, size, chunk_payload} - carries larger metadata or tool params when embedding directly.\\n6) CHECKPOINT: {stream_id, token, seq, signature, meta} - resume token emitted by server (or requested by client), short-lived.\\n7) FLOW_CONTROL: {stream_id, window_bytes} - client or server can adjust flow control.\\n8) ERROR_FRAME: {stream_id, seq, code, message} - terminal/non-terminal errors.\\n9) CLOSE_STREAM: {stream_id, reason} - end.\\n\\nNotes on STRUCT_FRAME and partial validation:\\n- The server can annotate which JSON path is completed in the current chunk so SDKs can run partial validators (e.g., \\\"title\\\" field done). We avoid sending large object parents until necessary.\\n- Clients should be able to subscribe to path-level events (SDK API will expose simple callbacks like onField(path, valuePart)).\\n\\nResume semantics and tokens:\\n- CHECKPOINT tokens are compact JWT-like strings signed by Redwood's streaming service with embedded: stream_id, last_seq, expiry, checksum of last N bytes.\\n- On reconnect, client re-OPENs with resume_token.       "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Streaming handshake, compact frames, and SDK resume - PRD (wip)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/product/hosted-api/streaming-handshake-compact-frames-and-sdk-resume-prd-wip.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: product-hosted-api\n\nper-customer.\\n\\nSDK ergonomics (JS/TS first-pass):\\n- Low-level: createStream(opts) returns AsyncIterable<Frame> and a controller with methods: send() (for client frames), requestResume(token), setWindow(bytes). This is for advanced use.\\n- High-level: StreamClient.open({schema, onText, onStruct, onTool, onCheckpoint, onError}) where handlers are simple sync/async functions. The SDK will manage checksums, resume attempts, and flow-control automatically.\\n- Tool registration: client.registerTool({id, handler: (params) => Promise<Result>, timeout}) - SDK routes TOOL_CALL frames to handlers. If no handler, SDK buffers until app decides.\\n- Validation mode: open|partial|strict. In partial mode, SDK emits onStruct events when enough path fragments arrive. In strict mode, SDK will attempt to reconstruct and run schema validation and emit error frames if mismatch.\\n\\nBackpressure and latency tradeoffs: \\n- Default client window 64KB. If app needs lower latency, pass max_window_bytes=8KB.\\n- SDK will apply jittered retries on resume to avoid thundering herd.\\n\\nSecurity & privacy considerations:\\n- Checkpoints should not include PII. If model output contains sensitive info, servers should redact before embedding into resume checksums.\\n- Tool-calls may include secrets in params; SDK must mark them ephemeral and not persist them in local storage unless explicitly requested by the app.\\n- Resume tokens must be signed and short-lived; no server-side sticky state required.\\n\\nTelemetry and observability (minimal):\\n- Events: stream.open, stream.resume_attempt, stream.resume_success, stream.resume_fail, tool.call, validation.failure, flow_control_change, stream.close.\\n- Recommended sample rates: resume events 100%, validation failures 100%, text_chunk histograms 1% by default.\\n\\nMigration and rollout plan:\\n- Phase 0 (internal): implement server v1 behind experiment flag + JS SDK prototype, test with 2 internal apps.\\n- Phase",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Streaming handshake, compact frames, and SDK resume - PRD (wip)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/product/hosted-api/streaming-handshake-compact-frames-and-sdk-resume-prd-wip.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: product-hosted-api\n\n.close.\\n- Recommended sample rates: resume events 100%, validation failures 100%, text_chunk histograms 1% by default.\\n\\nMigration and rollout plan:\\n- Phase 0 (internal): implement server v1 behind experiment flag + JS SDK prototype, test with 2 internal apps.\\n- Phase 1 (beta): opt-in customers, provide client library with feature flag header: X-RW-Stream-Pro: compact-v1.\\n- Phase 2 (GA): turn on for hosted-api streaming default for new models; provide backwards-compatible fallback that accepts plain newline-delimited text for older clients.\\n\\nOpen questions / TODOs:\\n- How large should CHECKPOINT's embedded checksum window be? (8KB vs 32KB?) - Eng to benchmark.\\n- Should DATA_BLOB be chunked separately (for large params) or force params_ref pattern to encourage pointer-based tool calls?\\n- UX for partial schema errors: should SDK automatically ask server for a re-generation or surface raw failure to the app?\\n- Interop with existing typed-tool-contracts (PRD cross-check needed).\\n\\nNext steps / action items:\\n- Miguel: prototype server framing layer and handshake negotiation (ENG-4821) - due 2025-12-08.\\n- Ava: JS SDK prototype (async iterator + high-level callback API) and sample app wiring for tool routing - due 2025-12-12.\\n- Priya (owner): Draft developer playbook + beta opt-in docs for Console and API docs, add telemetry events mapping - due 2025-12-18.\\n- Jordan: security review and resume token format design - due 2025-12-15.\\n\\nAppendix (sketch of handshake example):\\n1) Client -> POST /v1/streams (headers: X-RW-Stream-Pro: compact-v1, Accept: text/ndjson) body: OPEN_STREAM( {features:[\\\"resume\\\",\\\"schema_v1\\\"], schema_hash:\\\"sha256:abc\\\"} )\\n2) Server -> OPEN_ACK {stream",

Allows incremental validation.\\n4) TOOL_CALL: {seq, stream_id, tool_id, params_ref, confidence, meta} - indicates a candidate tool invocation. SDK may accept or reject. params_ref can be a small blob or pointer to a subsequent DATA_BLOB.\\n5) DATA_BLOB: {id, format:json|binary, size, chunk_payload} - carries larger metadata or tool params when embedding directly.\\n6) CHECKPOINT: {stream_id, token, seq, signature, meta} - resume token emitted by server (or requested by client), short-lived.\\n7) FLOW_CONTROL: {stream_id, window_bytes} - client or server can adjust flow control.\\n8) ERROR_FRAME: {stream_id, seq, code, message} - terminal/non-terminal errors.\\n9) CLOSE_STREAM: {stream_id, reason} - end.\\n\\nNotes on STRUCT_FRAME and partial validation:\\n- The server can annotate which JSON path is completed in the current chunk so SDKs can run partial validators (e.g., \\\"title\\\" field done). Content: Summary:

This doc proposes a compact streaming handshake and frame format to support low-latency token streams, structured tool-calls, and resumable sessions at the SDK level. The goal is a minimal server-client protocol that: reduces per-frame overhead, allows safe partial validation of structured outputs on the client, supports durable resume/checkpoint semantics for flaky networks, and keeps SDK ergonomics simple for product engineers.

Why this exists (motivation):
- Customers are building interactive experiences where partial results can trigger UI updates or downstream tool calls as soon as possible.
- Current streaming options either send raw deltas (fast but untyped) or large JSON blobs (safe but high latency).
- SDK authors want a single high-level API that works across: simple text streaming, structured JSON outputs, and tool call handoffs, without forcing app teams to re-implement complex resume and validation logic.

Primary goals:
- Compact frame model with typed frames (open, chunk, tool-call, checkpoint, error, close).
- Handshake negotiation for capabilities (schema validation, resume tokens, chunk checksums).
- SDK surface that exposes: an async iterator for low-level streaming, plus a high-level callback/handler model for tool frames and validated objects.
- A resumable checkpoint protocol that is idempotent and minimizes re-computation for client apps.
- Clear security and privacy constraints for tool-calls and checkpoint persistence.

Non-goals:
- Replacing full session storage / long-term logs (we aim for short-lived resume tokens, not permanent persistence).
- Complex on-server validation for every partial; server may annotate frames but client retains responsibility for final validation decisions.

Requirements (must-have):
- Negotiated frames: server and client can advertise supported frame types and version (v1).
- Frames are small and parseable without full JSON parse for the common text streaming path.
- Tool-call frames must include a minimal typed descriptor so SDKs can either route to a tool handler or buffer until validated.
- Checkpoints (resume tokens)

  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Unify minimal auth handshake and streamline streaming iterators across SDKs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/github\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/github/redwood/pr-173900-unify-minimal-auth-handshake-stream-wraps.json\nConnector: github\nWorkspace: redwood\n\nDescription: Motivation: SDKs had divergent lightweight auth handshakes and several slightly different async iterator APIs for streaming. This caused parity bugs (timeouts that only showed up in Go), awkward ergonomic differences in TypeScript consumer code, and duplicated retry logic. This PR introduces a small, intentionally minimal common handshake shim and a thin stream-wrapping adapter implemented in Python/TS/Go to normalize iterator behavior and retry policy wiring. Scope: - Add a minimal cross-language auth handshake contract (opaque token preflight + agreed timeout window) and adapters for each SDK. - Introduce StreamWrapper (Py/TS/Go) that presents a consistent async iterator/async generator/pull API and surfaces a single retry profile entrypoint. - Replace ad-hoc timeout and reauth calls in SDKs with the shim; preserve previous behavior as a compatibility opt-in via an explicit flag. - Bump SDK package versions: py 0.6.3 -> 0.6.4, ts 1.8.0 -> 1.8.1, go v1.3.1 -> v1.3.2. Messages: Alyssa: Quick sync on streaming handshake + launch criteria. Need a concrete decision on SSE vs WS, delta schema, and finish-reason semantics so we can lock SDK work.
Matt: My leaning is WS for v1 if we want multiplexing and client->server control messages. SSE is tempting for simplicity but limits two-way signals.
Ravi: Runtime view — WS gives us a stable channel for server-initiated control (cancels, model-switch). It costs more in connection mgmt but simplifies resume token mapping. SSE forces polling or separate control channel.
Jena: From SDK/mobile: SSE is easier for iOS background delivery but resume across flaky networks is harder. Web apps won't care as much.
Alyssa: Proposed compromise: API supports both transports from day 1, but we standardize a single handshake and delta contract so apps can swap transports without changing delta parsing. Handshake must include transport, delta_format, and resume preference.
Matt: Handshake example to be surfaced in docs:
```json
{ "transport": "ws", "delta_format": "json_ops", "resume": true, "client_version": "js-0.9.0" }
```
Ravi: We should enumerate finish reasons now. Minimal set: `completed`, `truncated` (token_limit), `cancelled` (client or server), `timeout` (SLO/window), `error` (internal). Add optional metadata: `truncated.reason` (e.g., max_tokens, safety), `error.code` if present.
Jena: UX acceptance: client must receive exactly one final finish event containing reason + final usage. Streaming must not emit an implicit final token after finish. Function calls should be delivered as discrete deltas `{type: "function_call", name, args}` so SDKs can surface them deterministically.
Alyssa: Launch gates checklist (high level):
- SDKs: JS, Python, iOS wrappers shipping streaming handshake + resume
- Server: handshake + session_id, per-connection rate limits, backpressure hooks
- Telemetry: p50/p95 latency for first delta, %sessions resumed, finish-reason distribution
- Docs: handshake examples",

# Adaptive connection handshake and graceful rollback for SDKs (Python/TS/Go)

Key: PM-891011

Team: product-management

Title: Adaptive connection handshake and graceful rollback for SDKs (Python/TS/Go)

Status: In Review

Priority: P1

Created At: 2026-02-10

Updated At: 2026-03-14

Creator: Ava Chen

Assignee: Diego Morales

Project: SDK Stability & Compat

Cycle: 2026-W06

Estimate: 8

Due Date: 2026-03-20

## Labels

- sdk
  - compatibility
  - streaming
  - pagination
  - backpressure
  - acceptance-criteria

Description: PRD-level requirements for an adaptive connection handshake and graceful rollback mechanism that standardizes how Redwood SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go) negotiate streaming capabilities, backpressure semantics, pagination cursors, and safe rollback behavior across client and runtime versions. Goal is a single compatibility contract that minimizes client breakage when server-side capabilities change and makes downgrade/resume predictable for customers with long-lived streams.

## Scope

- Define an explicit handshake protocol between SDK and Redwood runtime that advertises supported features: streaming modes (chunked vs evented), cursor formats, idempotency headers, backpressure windows, and retry semantics.
  - Specify client-side behavioral matrix for Python, TS, and Go SDKs when runtime responds with reduced capability (e.g., no streaming, truncated cursor format, reduced batch size).
  - Acceptance criteria and automated integration test harness (sdk-compat-suite) that runs cross-language scenarios including simulated network partitions and server capability downgrade.
  - Migration guidance and sample code for customers to opt into new handshake features while remaining compatible with older runtime versions.

Description: Motivation: SDKs had divergent lightweight auth handshakes and several slightly different async iterator APIs for streaming. This caused parity bugs (timeouts that only showed up in Go), awkward ergonomic differences in TypeScript consumer code, and duplicated retry logic. This PR introduces a small, intentionally minimal common handshake shim and a thin stream-wrapping adapter implemented in Python/TS/Go to normalize iterator behavior and retry policy wiring. Scope: - Add a minimal cross-language auth handshake contract (opaque token preflight + agreed timeout window) and adapters for each SDK. - Introduce StreamWrapper (Py/TS/Go) that presents a consistent async iterator/async generator/pull API and surfaces a single retry profile entrypoint. - Replace ad-hoc timeout and reauth calls in SDKs with the shim; preserve previous behavior as a compatibility opt-in via an explicit flag. - Bump SDK package versions: py 0.6.3 -> 0.6.4, ts 1.8.0 -> 1.8.1, go v1.3.1 -> v1.3.2. High level changes per SDK: - Python: new redwood.sdk.auth.minimal_handshake module (handshake.py), StreamWrapper class in redwood.sdk.streaming.adapter, small rework of async generator helpers, added unit tests and an integration test against the local dev runtime. - TypeScript: introduce compact handshake interface and streamWrap helper in src/stream/wrap.ts, exported types to improve TS ergonomics, adjust existing retry builder to accept the unified profile object. - Go: add handshake.go; implement stream adapter that exposes a channel-based iterator and a PullNext(ctx) method; adjust retry wiring to use the shared policy. Commits (summary): [1/5] introduce minimal auth contract and docs; [2/5] Python adapter + tests; [3/5] TypeScript adapter + types and examples; [4/5] Go adapter + channel iterator; [5/5] release bumps, changelogs, and cross-sdk integration test. Messages: Alyssa: Quick sync on streaming handshake + launch criteria. Need a concrete decision on SSE vs WS, delta schema, and finish-reason semantics so we can lock SDK work.
Matt: My leaning is WS for v1 if we want multiplexing and client->server control messages. SSE is tempting for simplicity but limits two-way signals.
Ravi: Runtime view — WS gives us a stable channel for server-initiated control (cancels, model-switch). It costs more in connection mgmt but simplifies resume token mapping. SSE forces polling or separate control channel.
Jena: From SDK/mobile: SSE is easier for iOS background delivery but resume across flaky networks is harder. Web apps won't care as much.
Alyssa: Proposed compromise: API supports both transports from day 1, but we standardize a single handshake and delta contract so apps can swap transports without changing delta parsing. Handshake must include transport, delta_format, and resume preference.
Matt: Handshake example to be surfaced in docs:
```json
{ "transport": "ws", "delta_format": "json_ops", "resume": true, "client_version": "js-0.9.0" }
```
Ravi: We should enumerate finish reasons now. Minimal set: `completed`, `truncated` (token_limit), `cancelled` (client or server), `timeout` (SLO/window), `error` (internal). Add optional metadata: `truncated.reason` (e.g., max_tokens, safety), `error.code` if present.
Jena: UX acceptance: client must receive exactly one final finish event containing reason + final usage. Streaming must not emit an implicit final token after finish. Function calls should be delivered as discrete deltas `{type: "function_call", name, args}` so SDKs can surface them deterministically.
Alyssa: Launch gates checklist (high level):
- SDKs: JS, Python, iOS wrappers shipping streaming handshake + resume
- Server: handshake + session_id, per-connection rate limits, backpressure hooks
- Telemetry: p50/p95 latency for first delta, %sessions resumed, finish-reason distribution
- Docs: handshake examples

SDK ergonomics (JS/TS first-pass):
- Low-level: createStream(opts) returns AsyncIterable<Frame> and a controller with methods: send() (for client frames), requestResume(token), setWindow(bytes). This is for advanced use.
- High-level: StreamClient.open({schema, onText, onStruct, onTool, onCheckpoint, onError}) where handlers are simple sync/async functions. The SDK will manage checksums, resume attempts, and flow-control automatically.
- Tool registration: client.registerTool({id, handler: (params) => Promise<Result>, timeout}) - SDK routes TOOL_CALL frames to handlers. If no handler, SDK buffers until app decides.
- Validation mode: open|partial|strict. In partial mode, SDK emits onStruct events when enough path fragments arrive. In strict mode, SDK will attempt to reconstruct and run schema validation and emit error frames if mismatch.

Backpressure and latency tradeoffs:

Motivation: several teams reported latency spikes and redundant reauth calls during bursty streaming workloads; debugging showed frequent credential refresh races and lack of a clean pause/resume lifecycle on client streams. Goals: 1) provide pausable stream primitives that preserve local cursor/offset state, allow explicit credential handoff with minimal RPC, and provide telemetry for retry decisioning; 2) harmonize ergonomic APIs across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs so examples and migration paths are consistent; 3) surface retry hints and a small set of typed retry presets to make opt-in behavior explicit. igor: ugh. For A we should treat numeric-like strings as numbers for those specific params. But we also don't want to silently accept totally invalid strings. Suggestion: heuristic coercion only for fields listed in a small whitelist (max_tokens, timeout_ms, top_k). Log a warning when coercion happens.

maya: +1. Add a lightweight coercion layer before validation: if param expects integer and value is a string of digits, coerce. Also update quickstart docs to show preferred input types.

Two fixes: (1) add embeddings.health to SDK surface in the next patch, (2) make the SDK return a clearer error when endpoint missing (hint: "endpoint may not be available in this SDK version; check server API or upgrade SDK").

noah: another subtle streaming mismatch: REST streams a chunk that begins with a newline when the model emits formatted markdown, but the Node SDK trims leading newlines from the first chunk before delivering to the app — so users see delayed newline. First-time devs think streaming is dropping characters.

maya: that's nasty. We should preserve chunk boundaries exactly for the first N bytes and avoid trimming. Add an e2e streaming test that asserts first chunk integrity.

igor: also spotted a race with auth refresh: SDK background refresh swaps tokens mid-stream causing a 401 on the next chunk; our retry logic then resends the entire request which results in duplicate side-effects for non-idempotent endpoints. Recommendation: don't retry streaming/mutating requests automatically after mid-stream 401. Instead surface a clear error and expose an option to use idempotency-key or resume tokens for safe retries.

Pricing sensitivity quick matrix (illustrative):
- Scenario A (Price -10%): volume increases +25% in 90 days, gross margin falls by ~9ppt if cost per token unchanged -> net burn up. Hiring recommendation: defer senior non-critical hires; increase monitoring cadence.
- Scenario B (Price flat): volume +8% -> manageable. Hiring: proceed with 25% of planned hires this quarter, defer remainder to next hiring window.
- Scenario C (Price +8%): volume -6% -> margin improves ~5ppt, runway +6 weeks. Hiring: green-light 60% of planned hires; prioritize mid-senior engineers.

How we translate price deltas to hiring gates (rule-of-thumb):
- For each 5% sustained drop in effective price, reduce planned hires by 10–15% (weighted towards non-core functions).
- For each 5% sustained increase, consider accelerating hires by 5–10% if pipeline velocity and candidate lead times justify.

Hiring priority buckets (shortlist for freeze/proceed decisions):
1) Critical (never freeze unless Tier 3): SRE, serving runtime, security, core infra.
2) High (evaluate case-by-case): model ops, platform performance, dedicated account engineering for committed customers.
3) Medium (first to pause): product teams not on guaranteed revenue paths, growth marketing.

-term contract hires for ops.
- Tier 3 (Critical): multiple signals + revenue realization below runway trigger (runway <10w). Actions: emergency exec review; prioritize survival hires only (SRE, customers at risk); consider limited feature rollback or temporary throughput throttles; start formal contingency planning for burn reduction.

Pricing sensitivity quick matrix (illustrative):
- Scenario A (Price -10%): volume increases +25% in 90 days, gross margin falls by ~9ppt if cost per token unchanged -> net burn up. Hiring recommendation: defer senior non-critical hires; increase monitoring cadence.
- Scenario B (Price flat): volume +8% -> manageable. Hiring: proceed with 25% of planned hires this quarter, defer remainder to next hiring window.
- Scenario C (Price +8%): volume -6% -> margin improves ~5ppt, runway +6 weeks. Hiring: green-light 60% of planned hires; prioritize mid-senior engineers.

How we translate price deltas to hiring gates (rule-of-thumb):
- For each 5% sustained drop in effective price, reduce planned hires by 10–15% (weighted towards non-core functions).
- For each 5% sustained increase, consider accelerating hires by 5–10% if pipeline velocity and candidate lead times justify.

Hiring priority buckets (shortlist for freeze/proceed decisions):
1) Critical (never freeze unless Tier 3): SRE, serving runtime, security, core infra.
2) High (evaluate case-by-case): model ops, platform performance, dedicated account engineering for committed customers.
3) Medium (first to pause): product teams not on guaranteed revenue paths, growth marketing.
4) Low (easy to pause): contractors, new grad cohorts, exploratory research hiring.

emits structured audit events for console and runbooks.
- Add shadowing toggles for parallel probing of candidate variants without impacting live split.
- Provide an auto-rollback policy with hysteresis and graduated backoff to avoid flapping.
- Expose diagnostic endpoints and Grafana panels for per-step metrics and rationale.

Design highlights and novel ideas:
- "Safepoints": explicit named checkpoints in a rollout where non-reversible expansion requires additional approval or stronger signals. Safepoints can be configured as time-based or metric-based.
- "Horizon decay": a configurable attenuation function that slows traffic growth if variance in key metrics increases; helps prevent step overshoot for bursty workloads.
- Quality-aware splits: traffic weights can be dynamically rebalanced by integrating a lightweight quality signal (e.g., rerank drift or semantic similarity) for A/B tests.
- Shadow probes: sampled requests are mirrored to candidate variants with separate budget accounting; failures in the shadow path do not affect the live split but surface in the supervisor's risk score.

Acceptance criteria:
1) POST /rollouts accepts new spec and validates schema, including safepoints and attenuation curve.
2) Supervisor advances steps automatically when configured SLOs are met for a configurable consecutive window, and pauses when the guardrail is violated.
3) Automatic rollback triggers when sustained regression (configurable window) exceeds threshold; rollback includes a cooldown to prevent immediate reattempt.
4) Shadowing mode can be enabled per-route and produced mirrored telemetry tracked independently.
5) E2E integration tests added that simulate latency spikes, error bursts, and quality regressions and assert supervisor behavior.
6) Grafana dashboard with per-step metrics and an "explain" view (why step advanced/paused/rolled back).",
